findings.headline: Investment income beat budget by 58%, though future returns will face headwind from delayed rate cuts.
findings.detail: Actual investment income reached £1.047m against budget of £0.664m across a £16.4m investment portfolio achieving 4.6% average return. This outperformance demonstrates active treasury management, but revised forecasts now expect the Bank Rate to remain elevated until Q3 2027 before any cuts, which will reduce future investment income.
findings.matters: Current treasury management is solid and helped offset capital losses, but the interest rate outlook suggests declining future investment returns. For a council planning to externalize £8.552m in borrowing, this compounds the borrowing cost pressure.
findings.figures: Actual £1.047m vs budget £0.664m; average return 4.6%
findings.quote: The Authority's budgeted investment income for the year was £0.664m. The actual investment income for the year was £1.047m.

findings.headline: Council is under-borrowed by £8.552m and plans to externalize this through PWLB when necessary.
findings.detail: The Council holds no external debt except a tractor hire purchase (April 2023). The £8.552m under-borrowing represents internal funding of waste collection vehicles and Blackwater Leisure Centre investment, which was agreed to be treated initially as internal borrowing with the expectation of later externalization.
findings.matters: This signals planned PWLB borrowing demand. Treasury advisers now forecast interest rates will hold elevated until Q3 2027, meaning when the council externalizes this borrowing it will face higher-than-previously-expected costs. Lenders need clarity on timing and amount.
findings.figures: £8.552m under-borrowed position
findings.quote: The Council is currently under-borrowed to a value of £8.552m. This means that the Council is using internal cash resources to fund borrowing which would otherwise need to be externalised (e.g. through PWLB borrowings). This value is attributable to the cost of waste collection vehicles and investment in the Blackwater Leisure Centre. These were agreed to be treated as internal borrowings initially, with the expectation of externalising that borrowing when necessary.

findings.headline: Strategic property funds have fallen in value to £4.532m from £5m invested, representing a £468k capital loss.
findings.detail: The Council holds £3m in CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund and £2m in Ninety-One Diversified Income Fund. Both funds experienced capital value declines during 2025/26 reflected in the year-end fair value. Although the funds generated £209k income, the capital loss of approximately £468k produces a net negative return for the year.
findings.matters: Capital losses on strategic investments reduce available reserves and financial resilience. Lenders assessing creditworthiness need to understand how the council's investment strategy has performed and what reserves are genuinely available for stress.
findings.figures: £4,532k fair value (down from £5m invested), £468k loss estimated
findings.quote: The falls in the capital values of the underlying assets were reflected in 31 March 2026 valuations of both funds. The Balance Sheet figure as at 31 March 2026 for long-term investments is recorded at fair value, £4,532k.

findings.headline: Temporary staffing spend significantly exceeded budget, indicating pressure to cover vacant permanent posts
findings.detail: Temporary and interim staffing cost £1.329m against a budget of £372k — a 3.5× overspend. The council achieved £114k savings by using the Essex County Council temporary staffing service (better rates than usual sector premiums), but this still leaves material unbudgeted cost. The paper notes that small councils find it difficult to leave posts vacant for extended periods, requiring interim cover.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted temporary staffing costs are a sign of structural staffing challenges — either difficulty in recruiting permanent staff, or inability to hold posts vacant long enough to deliver savings. This cost pressure compounds other budget pressures.
findings.figures: Actual £1.329m; budget £372k; net saving of £114k achieved through ECC service
findings.quote: In common with other small councils, it is often the case that vacant posts cannot be sustained for long and so interim staff are engaged to maintain service delivery.

findings.headline: Restructure brings large one-off costs including £833k pension strain from early retirements
findings.detail: As part of the Transforming Together restructure, the council incurred £301k in redundancy costs and £833k in pension strain (early retirement liabilities under LGPS terms). These are one-off, funded from reserves, but they represent significant cash movements. The council notes the costs are nearly identical to a similar restructure seven years earlier.
findings.matters: A lender tracking cash and reserves needs to see major one-off pension liabilities. A £833k pension strain cost signals the council was offering or honouring early-departure terms as part of restructuring — a known source of unfunded liability.
findings.figures: Redundancy £301k; pension strain £833k; one-off support costs £170k
findings.quote: Redundancy total is £301,000. Pension strain total is £833,000. One-off support costs amount to £170k.

findings.headline: Large drawdown of reserves to fund Local Government Reorganisation restructuring, creating uncertainty during a period of structural change
findings.detail: Of the £1.373m increase in staffing budgets, £1.084m is funded from reserves — specifically for posts needed to wind down Maldon District Council and prepare for the new Mid-Essex unitary authority. The council is also funding one-off restructure costs (£301k redundancy, £833k pension strain, £170k support) through reserves. In total, an application of £4.854m from reserves is proposed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of reserves. During Local Government Reorganisation (March 2026 decision, ongoing workstreams), a council is depleting buffers to fund both restructuring and preparation work. This creates cash pressure at a time of institutional uncertainty, and leaves fewer reserves to absorb unexpected costs during transition.
findings.figures: £1.084m of pay increase funded from reserves for LGR; total reserve application £4.854m (£1.072m revenue + £3.782m capital)
findings.quote: £1.084m is funded from reserves to support posts identified as required through preparation for LGR (either to ensure MDC is wound-up in an orderly way, or to help with preparation for reorganisation itself)

findings.headline: Finance Services directorate overspent by £410k due to corporate savings targets that were included in prior-year budgets but not delivered
findings.detail: The Finance directorate shows a £410k overspend. The paper attributes this directly to unachieved corporate savings targets embedded in the baseline: £281k for vacancy factor (see above) and £120k for senior officer savings. This suggests budget plans for 2025/26 and beyond included targets that may not be deliverable.
findings.matters: Overspends in the finance function itself signal budget planning or delivery issues at the core. If corporate savings targets built into budgets are routinely unachieved, future budget forecasts are less credible.
findings.figures: £410k overspend in Finance Services; £281k vacancy factor + £120k senior officer savings
findings.quote: The overspend in Finance Services is due to prior years' corporate savings targets being included in these budgets. These savings include £281k for 'vacancy factor' savings and £120k for senior officer savings. Vacancy factor savings have been unachieved.

findings.headline: Unachieved vacancy factor savings expose a core budget control mechanism as unviable in a small council
findings.detail: Maldon budgeted £281k in savings from holding posts vacant, but these savings were not delivered. The council states explicitly that in small authorities, vacant posts cannot be left unfilled because service continuity requires interim cover. The paper includes a footnote saying that securing savings through vacancy factor "is not a viable approach" — a fundamental shift in how this council can plan future budgets.
findings.matters: A lender assessing a council's ability to deliver budget plans needs to know if a key savings mechanism (vacancy factor) is off the table. If Maldon cannot hold posts vacant without service impact, future savings targets become harder to hit and less reliable.
findings.figures: £281k budgeted, unachieved
findings.quote: Vacancy factor savings have been unachieved. This is because vacant posts usually require cover to ensure service continuity, a more urgent issue in a small council.

findings.headline: Council has historical recruitment difficulty for key roles and is budgeting staff investment to mitigate turnover risk during LGR transition
findings.detail: Council notes it 'has sometimes struggled to recruit key roles, a fact sometimes attributable to geography and accessibility or to scale and challenge.' It responds by budgeting salary growth (£540k in 2026-27, £450k in 2027-28) stating that 'Investing in staff becomes a pull or retention factor to mitigate this risk, while disinvestment could become a push factor.'
findings.matters: Staff retention challenges ahead of reorganisation create service delivery and financial control risk; inability to recruit/retain key finance and management roles could compromise financial stewardship.
findings.quote: Maldon has sometimes struggled to recruit key roles, a fact sometimes attributable to geography and accessibility or to scale and challenge, etc. Investing in staff becomes a 'pull' or retention factor to mitigate this risk, while disinvestment could become a 'push' factor.

findings.headline: Reorganisation into unitary authority in April 2028 creates liability transfer uncertainty while council plans new borrowing
findings.detail: The MTFS is structured around Maldon's planned dissolution on 1 April 2028. The council projects finances through 2028-29 (after reorganisation) assuming all investments are approved and £10m external borrowing is taken. It is unclear whether the successor unitary authority will be contractually bound by Maldon's debt obligations.
findings.matters: New borrowing ahead of organisational dissolution creates legal uncertainty about debt holders' recourse; the successor body may not inherit or be liable for predecessor obligations.
findings.figures: Reorganisation date 1 April 2028; MTFS extends through 2028-29
findings.quote: The MTFS is prepared on the basis that Greater Essex will be reorganised into 3, 4, or 5 unitary councils from 1 April 2028.

findings.headline: Government funding settlement confirms real-terms reduction of £600k to 2028/29 due to post-2020 redistribution
findings.detail: The December 2025 settlement shows core spending power reducing from £11.7m to £11.1m. The council notes this reflects adjustment of historically above-average funding as government pursues 'fair funding' to benefit more deprived areas. Maldon's funding per person has been higher than average and is being corrected downward.
findings.matters: Structural funding reduction combined with above-inflation cost pressures (4-5% per year) forces councils to find recurring savings or deplete reserves; Maldon has chosen reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Core spending power reduces from £11.7m (2025-26) to £11.1m (2028-29), a reduction of £600k
findings.quote: This settlement shows that anticipated core spending power (the main elements of council funding from government) will reduce from £11.6m in the current year to £11.3m by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Council uses reserves to fund recurring revenue growth rather than achieving savings balance
findings.detail: The MTFS states 'It is assumed that revenue growth is funded from reserves.' New recurrent pressures (£1.3m in 2026-27, £1.2m in 2027-28) exceed new savings (£0.5m and £0.8m respectively), with the gap covered by reserve drawdown. This approach is only sustainable while reserves exist.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover recurring spending gaps indicates the council cannot balance operations from its own revenue, which becomes acute after LGR when reserves may be split or unavailable.
findings.figures: Reserve funding for growth £1,451k (2026-27); new pressures exceed new savings by £774k (2026-27) and £375k (2027-28)
findings.quote: It is assumed that revenue growth is funded from reserves.

findings.headline: Growing leisure contract cost pressures rising to £514k in 2027/28
findings.detail: The reserves forecast shows increasing unfunded costs from the leisure contract: £183k in 2026/27 rising to £514k in 2027/28. These costs are being absorbed through reserve drawdown rather than budget reallocation or contract renegotiation.
findings.matters: Growing contract costs not addressed through savings indicate either poor contract management or service delivery problems that signal wider financial distress.
findings.figures: Leisure contract pressures: £183k (2026-27), £514k (2027-28)
findings.quote: Leisure contract (183)... Leisure contract (514)

findings.headline: Council plans £10m external borrowing in 2027/28 while reserves deplete from £10.5m to negative £7.6m
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts usable reserves declining from £10.5m at start of 2026/27 to £322k at start of 2027/28, then to negative £7.6m by 2028/29. Within this, the council will externalise £10m of borrowing in 2027/28. This reserve depletion is explicitly planned as part of capital investment and LGR preparation strategy.
findings.matters: A council taking on £10m of new external borrowing while simultaneously depleting reserves and approaching structural reorganisation presents repayment risk; the successor unitary authority may not assume all liabilities.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £10.5m (2026-27 start) declining to negative £7.6m (2028-29 start); £10m external borrowing externalised 2027/28
findings.quote: The model also assumes that £10m of borrowing is externalised in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 9c Capital & Investment, Min Revenue Provision and Treasury Management 2026-27
findings.headline: Blackwater Leisure Centre investment was approved for 2025/26 without a detailed programme of works, causing slippage to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council included investment in Blackwater Leisure Centre in the 2025/26 capital budget before identifying what works would be undertaken. As a result, some of the works originally planned for 2025/26 have been carried forward to 2026/27. This represents a process failure: capital was approved for a specific project without the basic scoping to make that approval meaningful.
findings.matters: Approving capital expenditure before knowing what it will deliver demonstrates weak project governance and increases risk of further delays and cost escalation, which are material concerns for lenders assessing financial control discipline
findings.figures: Works rephased from 2025/26 to 2026/27 (within the £3,966k leisure centre spending in 2025/26)
findings.quote: This investment was included for 2025/26 before a detailed programme of works had been identified, with the result that some of the works planned for 2025/26 have been carried forward to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Base budget pressures of £0.819m from inflation and technical adjustments force choice between service cuts or reserve depletion.
findings.detail: Net impact of pay and price growth plus technical adjustments created £0.819m additional budget pressure before any growth bids. Council chose to maintain service levels using reserves rather than reduce services, accelerating reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Inability to absorb base cost inflation within existing CSP signals structural mismatch between funding and costs; strategy depends on reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: £0.819m net pressure from inflation and technical changes
findings.quote: This shows that the net impact of technical adjustments and pay and price inflation is additional pressures of £0.819m. Growth in the budgets for goods and services (contractors and suppliers) is notable.

findings.headline: Waste contract costs inflating above background inflation, partially offset by rising Extended Producer Responsibility grant.
findings.detail: The council identifies waste collection contract inflation as a specific pressure within goods and services budgets, noting it 'tends to be above background inflation'. EPR grant is increasing from £648k to £694k, providing partial offset, but structural pressure on waste costs remains.
findings.matters: Ongoing above-inflation cost pressures in waste indicate contractual or service-delivery challenges and may recur; offsetting grant is time-limited.
findings.figures: Waste contract growth cited as above-background inflation; EPR grant £648k (2025/26) to £694k (2026/27)
findings.quote: Growth in the budgets for goods and services (contractors and suppliers) is notable. This is due to a combination of technical changes (where grant funding and supplier costs were previously netted off but are now separated in line with best practice) and inflationary pressures, including the inflation in the cost of the waste contract (which tends to be above background inflation).

findings.headline: £1m earmarked for Local Government Reorganisation preparation, but council acknowledges uncertainty over actual costs required.
findings.detail: The council has provided £1m in earmarked reserves for LGR preparation costs, but states 'it is not yet clear if the full £1m will be required'. However, early indications from officers and Chief Executives across Greater Essex suggest 'potential cost pressures may be significant'. This represents both a commitment and a hedge against unknown costs.
findings.matters: LGR cost uncertainty creates contingency risk; actual costs could exceed provision, requiring additional reserve drawdown or borrowing.
findings.figures: £1m earmarked for LGR preparation
findings.quote: It is not yet clear if the full £1m will be required, but early indications from the discussions of officers and Chief Executives across Greater Essex are that potential cost pressures may be significant and should be provided for.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves forecast to deplete significantly, with £10m external borrowing required to avoid deficit by 2028/29.
findings.detail: Starting 2026/27 with £5.039m general reserves, the council forecasts these falling to £1.604m by end of 2027/28, then requiring external borrowing of £10m in 2027/28 to avoid going negative. The reserve depletion is driven by intentional strategy to fund growth and maintenance rather than cut services ahead of Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion and dependency on external borrowing indicates weakening balance sheet position and reduces financial resilience.
findings.figures: General reserves: £5.039m (2026/27 start), £1.604m (2027/28 start), requires £10m borrowing to avoid deficit
findings.quote: The estimates include an assumed £10m of external borrowing to be undertaken in 2027/28, although the amount and the timing is not yet known with certainty. The overall position retains £2.6m of 'core' reserves as a result.

findings.headline: Council planning first-time external borrowing of £10m in 2027/28, moving from current zero borrowing position.
findings.detail: Maldon currently has no external borrowing and is one of only two councils in Greater Essex without any. The budget assumes £10m of external borrowing in 2027/28, representing a material shift in treasury strategy. This is being driven by reserve depletion plans and the need to fund capital and revenue gaps.
findings.matters: First entry into external borrowing is a significant change in council's financial structure and debt position; lenders need to assess sustainability of this new obligation.
findings.figures: £10m assumed borrowing 2027/28; currently zero borrowing; Greater Essex average £250m (excluding outliers)
findings.quote: At present, the council has no external borrowing. The decision to use external borrowing has been taken, in principle, in the approval of Council given to the 2025/26 Treasury Management Strategy in its meeting of February 2025. This budget sets out that external borrowing is now expected (but not yet confirmed).

findings.headline: Government Core Spending Power reducing by 2.5% over three years, driven by population revaluation and deprivation weighting.
findings.detail: Core Spending Power is forecast to fall from £11.6m in 2025/26 to £11.3m by 2028/29. The council describes this as 'material reduction' and was a key driver of the budget strategy decision to use reserves rather than cut services.
findings.matters: Structural reduction in government funding is a core indicator of council fiscal sustainability and debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £11.6m (current year) to £11.3m (2028/29); 2.5% reduction in real terms
findings.quote: The headline for Maldon is the material reduction in resources. This is driven by the updating of population data for all councils, plus the greater profile given to deprivation indications in the allocations to individual councils. Figure 2 clearly shows a reduction from CSP of £11.6m in the current year to £11.3m in 2028/29. This is a 2.5% reduction applied in real terms.

findings.headline: Blackwater Leisure Centre capital works slipped from 2025/26 to 2026/27; revised budget £3.97m realised only £2.62m spend
findings.detail: The Blackwater Leisure Centre investment was included in the 2025/26 budget before a detailed programme of works had been identified. This led to a revised budget of £3,966k producing only £2,620k forecast spend in 2025/26, forcing unexecuted works to be carried forward to 2026/27 (budgeted £3,522k).
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's capital programme is slipping behind schedule due to poor planning, raising questions about project delivery capability and execution risk across the £11.2m capital investment plan
findings.figures: Revised budget £3,966k, forecast spend £2,620k (2025/26); deferred to 2026/27 budget £3,522k
findings.quote: This investment was included for 2025/26 before a detailed programme of works had been identified, with the result that some of the works planned for 2025/26 have been carried forward to 2026/27.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance increased by £187k while earmarked reserves declined
findings.detail: Unallocated reserves grew from £8,636k to £8,823k (+£187k) despite earmarked reserves falling by £871k overall. This suggests the council is building flexible financial capacity while spending down specific-purpose reserves as planned.
findings.matters: Growing unallocated reserves indicate strengthening general financial flexibility and capacity to absorb unexpected pressures
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £8,636k to £8,823k (+£187k); Total earmarked reserves: £6,570k to £5,698k (-£871k)
findings.quote: Unallocated - available for any purpose

findings.headline: Transformation reserve being actively used for change programmes
findings.detail: The transformation reserve fell from £928k to £729k with £199k drawn during the year (£12k in July, £187k in October). This reflects ongoing investment in service improvement and restructuring initiatives.
findings.matters: Active transformation spending indicates the council is investing in operational change, which affects both near-term budget impact and future cost base
findings.quote: Transformation

findings.headline: Infrastructure and planning reserve depleted by £233k in planned draw-down
findings.detail: The CIL and Local Development Plan review reserve fell from £506k to £273k, with £233k released in June for planned spending. This represents a 46% reduction in this specific fund during the year.
findings.matters: CIL reserves fund infrastructure and development work; significant annual drawdown shows major planned activities but also indicates the council is spending this strategic resource rapidly
findings.quote: Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and Local Development Plan (LDP) review

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision of £496k introduced in October budget revisions
findings.detail: The original budget contained no MRP provision, but the revised budget includes £496k for Minimum Revenue Provision (the accounting charge for debt repayment), added in the October S&R revision. MRP is mandated when councils have borrowing, suggesting new debt arrangements were agreed mid-year.
findings.matters: Introduction of £496k annual MRP creates an ongoing revenue commitment to service debt, reducing funds available for services and directly affecting the council's financial capacity and borrowing headroom.
findings.figures: MRP: £0k original, £496k revised (October addition)

findings.headline: Council drawing £244k from General Fund to balance revised budget
findings.detail: The revised budget includes a £244k draw from General Fund (transfer shown in funding section), whereas the original budget had no such draw. This indicates the council is supplementing its government grant, council tax, and business rate income with reserve drawdown to cover expenditure.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing revenue expenditure suggests structural imbalance between income and costs, a key indicator of financial stress that lenders track when assessing council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: General Fund transfer: £0k original, £244k revised
findings.quote: Transfer (from) / to General Fund 0  (55) (119) (70) (244)

findings.headline: Finance service expenditure increased from £156k to £1,039k in mid-year budget revisions
findings.detail: The Finance sub-directorate budget increased by £883k in the revised budget (£156k original to £1,039k revised), driven by £778k added in July S&R committee and £105k in October S&R. This is by far the largest absolute and proportional increase of any service area in the reconciliation, suggesting significant unplanned financial demand.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council finances would want to understand what drove this exceptional increase in finance costs, as it signals either major unforeseen financial challenges or significant commitments affecting the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Finance: £156k original, £1,039k revised; July £778k addition, October £105k addition

findings.headline: Car parking project showing cost inflation of £37k due to delays, funded through partnership income
findings.detail: The car parking project, originally approved in 2022/23, has experienced increased material and labour costs due to project delays. The revised budget of £158k is now forecast to outturn at £195k. The council is managing this cost overrun using income from the South Essex Parking Partnership.
findings.matters: Cost inflation on capital projects indicates pricing pressure risk; this case shows the council can manage it through available income, though delays and cost increases suggest either poor initial project planning or external cost pressures affecting delivery.
findings.figures: £37k overspend; revised budget £158k; forecast outturn £195k
findings.quote: delays have meant that the material and labour costs have increased, funding is available using the South Essex Parking Partnership (SEPP) income we received.

findings.headline: Leisure centre investment of £5.8m to be drawn over two years after project works commenced in August 2025
findings.detail: Works on phase 1 of the leisure centre project started on 18 August 2025. The council originally budgeted £4m as a loan facility with no known start date. It now forecasts £2.6m spending in 2025/26, with the remaining £3.2m loan drawdown to Places Leisure expected in 2026/27, totalling £5.8m.
findings.matters: A significant borrowing commitment (£5.8m, 45% larger than the original £4m budget) affects the council's debt profile, interest costs, and treasury cash flow, particularly given the phased drawdown extending into the next financial year.
findings.figures: £5.8m total facility; £2.6m forecast 2025/26; £3.2m forecast 2026/27; original budget £4m
findings.quote: The remaining loan drawdown to Places Leisure of £3.2m (£5.8m in total) is expected in the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: Council commits £45,000 with acknowledged financial risk that repayment is not guaranteed
findings.detail: The council proposes to underwrite 50% of a national music artist's performance (£45,000), expecting full repayment through ticket sales and parking income from approximately 14,000 tickets. The document explicitly states repayment 'is not guaranteed' and depends on ticket sales and secondary spend, though officers believe recovery is 'likely' based on 2024 precedent when Soultasia generated £842,886 in tourism spending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is making discretionary financial commitments with downside risk to reserves if event revenues underperform
findings.figures: £45,000 commitment; 14,000 tickets anticipated; £965,346.20 potential economic return; 2024 Soultasia generated £842,886.46 in tourism spending
findings.quote: Whilst it is not guaranteed, it is likely that the underwritten cost will be recouped either in full or extremely close to the £45,000 commitment. This will be dependent on ticket sales and on secondary spend such as managed parking.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing for Leisure capital will reduce investment income by £185k per annum
findings.detail: By using treasury investments to fund the Leisure project, the council forgoes investment income on those sums. At Link's projected interest rate of 3.25%, this represents £185k per annum in lost revenue, a material reduction in the council's investment-derived income.
findings.matters: Lost investment income directly reduces revenue available for services and reserves, affecting the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £185k per annum; based on interest rate of c.3.25%
findings.quote: The resulting loss of investment income is estimated at £185k pa (per annum) based on Link's current projected interest rates of c.3.25%

findings.headline: New Leisure contract will require £5.713m capital investment over three years, funded by drawing down treasury investments
findings.detail: The council is planning to sign a new Leisure contract that assumes £5.713m in capital investment spread across 2025/26–2027/28. Rather than external borrowing, this will be funded through internal borrowing—temporarily using the council's own treasury investments to cover the capital costs.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand how major capital commitments are funded and how they affect the council's reserves and cash position.
findings.figures: £5.713m capital investment over 3 years; internal borrowing of £4.0m (2025/26), £1.0m (2026/27), £0 (2027/28)
findings.quote: The contract assumes capital investment of £5.713m over the next 3-years. This will be funded from internal borrowing. i.e. temporarily utilising the Council's treasury investments.

findings.headline: Council will deplete its £24.1m invested reserves to fund capital projects and contingency budget gaps
findings.detail: The council intends to finance new waste vehicles and leisure centre investments through internal borrowing, drawing down invested reserves. The council also signals that reserves may be needed to cover future budget gaps. Invested balances will decrease over time from the current £24.1m as these demands are met.
findings.matters: Drawing down capital reserves for both fixed capital projects and contingency budget funding reduces financial headroom and could constrain future borrowing capacity if reserves become materially depleted.
findings.figures: Invested balances: £24.1m at period end; increased by £5.0m from April to September 2025
findings.quote: As a result, invested balances will, over time, decrease because capital receipts and internal borrowing will be used to finance capital expenditure. In addition, reserves may be used to cover any future budget gaps.

findings.headline: Council briefly exceeded prudential indicator limit on its operational bank account in H1
findings.detail: The council breached a bank operational account limit during the first half of 2025/26. The Section 151 Officer describes this as brief and confirms that only one prudential indicator was breached overall. The specific cause or duration of the breach is not detailed in the report.
findings.matters: Breaches of prudential indicators indicate control failures in cash forecasting and management, raising questions about whether the council can effectively monitor and control its cash position.
findings.figures: One prudential indicator briefly breached
findings.quote: The Prudential Indicators for 2025 / 26, which were set on 15 February 2024 as part of the Treasury Management Strategy Statement shown at Table 1 above have been complied with to date, except for some brief breached bank limits that occurred on the Council's current account, disclosed below.

findings.headline: Capital investment profile revised mid-year, generating £231k additional interest income
findings.detail: The council has revised its capital investment profile during the year, resulting in higher cash balances than budgeted. This generates an additional £231k in forecast interest income compared to the revised budget, with the surplus flowing to the General Fund Balance.
findings.matters: Revising capital plans mid-year may signal financing constraints or changed priorities. It affects the council's service delivery capacity and long-term capital resilience, and raises questions about what spending was deferred and why.
findings.figures: Investment Income variance £231k favourable
findings.quote: Due to revised capital investment profile during the year, the forecast for the interest income is forecast to be higher with the surplus going to the General Fund Balance.

findings.headline: Revenue and Benefits salary costs of £182k being funded from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The Customer Services & Operations directorate is forecasting an overspend of £158k for the year. Within this, revenue and benefits staff costs have exceeded budget, requiring the council to fund this £182k shortfall from earmarked reserves rather than from operating income. Parks salaries also show an additional cost of £59k.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover recurring salary costs suggests the council cannot sustainably fund its current staffing from operating income, indicating a structural budget problem rather than a one-off issue.
findings.figures: £158k overspend (Customer Services & Operations), £182k salary costs funded from reserves, £59k Parks salary additional cost
findings.quote: Revenue and benefits salary costs £182k to be funded from earmarked reserves and £59k additional cost of Parks salaries.

findings.paper_title: 10 Financial Year 2026-27 Budget Proposals and MTFS Update
findings.headline: Economic outlook has worsened since budget assumptions were set, risking deeper funding cuts than the assumed 10%
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that the economic outlook has remained challenging or worsened since the Fair Funding consultation, and that future resource reductions may exceed current expectations.
findings.matters: Budget assumptions may already be optimistic, with downside risk of funding cuts deeper than the 10% already factored in.
findings.figures: None specified; references potential cuts beyond the assumed 10%
findings.quote: Since that consultation, the economic outlook has remained challenging if not worsened. This may lead to future resource reductions that exceed current expectations.

findings.paper_title: 10 Financial Year 2026-27 Budget Proposals and MTFS Update
findings.headline: Recruitment and retention challenges expected to persist through April 2028 local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council faces an ongoing challenging recruitment environment in some services, with added uncertainty as LGR approaches and staff consider their future interests. The employment offer must remain competitive.
findings.matters: Staff instability during reorganisation could increase costs if competitive pay pressures persist while managing budget pressures.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided
findings.quote: An on-going challenging recruitment environment in some services, this is likely to continue to be uncertain as LGR approaches and staff consider the future interests.

findings.paper_title: 10 Financial Year 2026-27 Budget Proposals and MTFS Update
findings.headline: District government funding expected to fall by up to 10% with flat cash thereafter
findings.detail: Early warning indicates district councils may see funding reductions of up to 10% in some areas, followed by 'flat cash' (zero inflation) in 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.matters: A 10% external funding cut with no inflation protection removes flexibility to avoid service reductions or deeper reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Up to 10% reduction; flat cash position in following two years
findings.quote: Early warning has been given that resources for districts may fall by up to 10% in some areas, with a 'flat cash' (zero inflation) position in the following two years.

findings.paper_title: 10 Financial Year 2026-27 Budget Proposals and MTFS Update
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves to fall from £6.6m to £0.3m in a single financial year
findings.detail: The council plans to draw down earmarked reserves by £2.6m for the revenue gap, £0.5m for repairs and renewals, and up to £2.5m for capital investment in a worst-case scenario, reducing them to just £0.3m by March 2027.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion to £0.3m leaves minimal buffer for unforeseen pressures and severely constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £6.6m starting position; £0.3m projected; £2.6m revenue gap draw, £0.5m repairs, £2.5m capital (worst case)
findings.quote: Currently it is anticipated that there will be a significant drawdown of Earmarked Reserves to balance the revenue budget gap, consistent with previous years' MTFS.

findings.paper_title: 10 Financial Year 2026-27 Budget Proposals and MTFS Update
findings.headline: Revenue gap grows from £0.694m to £1.290m over three years, to be funded from reserves
findings.detail: The council faces an unresolved structural deficit. Before growth bids, the gap is £0.694m in 2026/27, widening to £0.893m in 2027/28 and £1.290m in 2028/29. This must be funded from reserves under current assumptions rather than balanced from revenue sources.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit signals the council cannot balance its budget from ongoing revenue sources and increasingly depends on finite reserve draws.
findings.figures: £0.694m, rising to £1.290m by 2028/29; gap of £0.893m in year 2
findings.quote: The current position shows a gap before growth bids of £0.694m, rising to £1.290m by 2028/29. In common with previous financial plans, this will need to be funded from reserves unless other funding sources were available.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves reduced from £6.6m to £5.7m despite receiving additional Q2 grants — indicating substantial allocation of reserves
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves fell by £0.9m despite the council receiving additional revenue grants in Q2 that are being transferred into the earmarked reserve. This indicates material drawdown of earmarked reserves through unspecified 'decisions to allocate reserves'. Total reserves declined from £15.2m to £14.5m across the year position.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown activity is a key indicator of financial resilience and how the council is funding commitments. A £0.9m reduction in earmarked reserves after accounting for new grants suggests active use of reserves to meet planned obligations or emerging needs.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £6.6m to £5.7m (£0.9m reduction); total reserves: £15.2m to £14.5m; core reserve retained: £2.3m
findings.quote: Further to some decisions to allocate reserves and the proposed transfer of additional revenue grants received in Q2 to an earmarked reserve, the current position shows earmarked reserves as £5.7m, and general reserves £8.8m

findings.headline: Capital programme delivering only £5,234k against revised budget of £6,550k — a 20% underspend
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a capital programme underspend of £1,316k. This represents a material shortfall of 20% against the revised capital budget, with the document deferring detailed reasons to Appendix 2. This level of slippage suggests either delivery delays on specific schemes or changed priorities.
findings.matters: A 20% capital shortfall affects the council's ability to deliver planned services and infrastructure, and signals potential delivery or funding constraints that a lender would need to understand when assessing the council's operational capability.
findings.figures: £5,234k actual delivery against £6,550k revised budget; underspend of £1,316k (20%)
findings.quote: the forecast for the capital budget projects an underspend of £1,316k against the revised 2025/26 Capital programme of £6,550k

findings.headline: Transformation Reserve being drawn down to fund cemetery management system
findings.detail: £70,000 is being transferred from the Transformation Reserve to implement a digital solution for cemetery records and burial mapping. This depletes reserves held for change initiatives to fund what appears to be a support system.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion for operational systems reduces financial flexibility for other council priorities and may indicate insufficient revenue budgets for IT and cemetery services.
findings.quote: To implement a digital solution for the Councils Cemeteries service, burial records and maps for plotting graves. The project costs include both the software, implementation and project resource costs

findings.headline: Car parking capital spending is forecast to overrun by £30k (22% variance)
findings.detail: Car parking expenditure is budgeted at £137k but forecast to spend £167k, a variance of £30k. This represents a 22% cost overrun on the car parking project, though the spending is funded through South Essex Parking Partnership funding.
findings.matters: Cost overruns, even when funded, indicate potential planning issues or scope changes and are worth understanding in terms of project delivery and future cost control.
findings.figures: Car Parking budget £137k, forecast outturn £167k, variance £30k
findings.quote: Car Parking 137 167 30 South Essex Parking Partnership Funding (incl b/fwd funding)

findings.headline: Internal borrowing funds 61% of the capital programme, with capital receipts contributing only 22%
findings.detail: The £6.51m capital programme is funded with £4m internal borrowing (61%), £1.44m capital receipts (22%), £541k grants (8%), £363k s.106 contributions (6%), and £274k budget carried forward (4%). This indicates limited capital receipts generation and substantial reliance on reserve drawdown to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: A capital programme heavily dependent on internal borrowing signals reserve depletion risk and constrains future borrowing capacity, which affects the council's financial resilience and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Internal Borrowing £4,000k; Total Capital Programme £6,510k; Capital Receipts Applied £1,439k
findings.quote: Internal Borrowing 4,000 4,000 0

findings.headline: Maldon increased planned reserve draws by £293k to £366k total to balance its 2025-26 budget
findings.detail: The council originally budgeted £73k draw from earmarked reserves but revised this upward to £166k. Additionally, £200k from general fund draw was added (zero in original budget). Both increases came through mid-year adjustments in June and July, suggesting either initial budgeting was unrealistic or unforeseen costs emerged during the year.
findings.matters: Increasing reserve draws mid-year indicates the council cannot fully fund planned spending from grant income and council tax alone, signalling budget pressure and reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserve revised draw: £166k (from £73k); General fund revised draw: £200k (from £0); Total net expenditure rise: £12,416k to £12,709k
findings.quote: Transfer (from) / to Earmarked Reserve (73) (132) (17) 56 (166); Transfer (from) / to General Fund 0 (55) (145) (200)

findings.headline: Total useable reserves decline by £290,200 to £14.91m, with general fund reduced to £8.44m.
findings.detail: Across all reserves, the council moves from £15.20m to £14.91m, with unallocated general fund falling from £8.64m to £8.44m. However, the council designates £2.3m of the general fund explicitly for cashflow contingency, leaving approximately £6.1m flexible.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion over time suggests either structural budget pressure or planned use to smooth service delivery; the trend and adequacy of remaining unallocated reserves matters for assessing financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Total Useable Reserves £15,204,921 to £14,914,721 (reduction £290,200); General Fund £8,636,024 to £8,436,524
findings.quote: Unallocated - available for any purpose. Of the total, £2.3m to be retained to support cashflow variations and as a provision 'of last resort'.

findings.headline: Place Leisure contract costs remain unconfirmed 18 months after April 2024 finalisation
findings.detail: A major service outsourcing contract finalised in April 2024 still has no confirmed revenue or capital costs for the current year. The forecast incorporates November 2024 financial implications but defers final cost confirmation to the next quarterly update.
findings.matters: A major contract this far into delivery should have settled costs. Ongoing uncertainty after 18 months suggests scope or pricing issues that could result in material budget variations.
findings.figures: Costs deferred for confirmation in next quarterly update
findings.quote: The contract was finalised in April 2024 and revenue and capital costs for the current year are not yet confirmed. These will be included in the next quarterly update to the Committee

findings.headline: De-silting works excluded from forecast with methodology, timeframe and costs still being identified
findings.detail: The forecast explicitly excludes de-silting works, which represents a known liability to the council but with cost and timing unquantified. This is flagged as pending identification of methodology, timeframe and cost.
findings.matters: Unquantified capital or maintenance liabilities create hidden budget pressure that will eventually require reserve drawdown or contingency borrowing once scope is established.
findings.figures: Amount and timeline unquantified
findings.quote: This revenue forecast excludes the impact of de-silting works, as a clear methodology, timeframe, and costs are still being identified

findings.headline: Chief Financial Officer and deputy both vacant, with unsuccessful prior recruitment attempt
findings.detail: The Finance budget shows a £52k overspend (5.6% of £934k) driven entirely by interim staff costs to cover vacant CFO and deputy positions. The document notes an unsuccessful attempt to recruit a permanent deputy, suggesting structural issues with the role.
findings.matters: A council without a permanent CFO or deputy creates continuity risk and control weakness in financial management. Repeated recruitment failure indicates either salary insufficiency or role design problems that will persist.
findings.figures: Finance overspend £52k (5.6% of budget)
findings.quote: Ongoing interim costs to cover vacant posts (CFO and deputy) plus additional costs to progress recruitment of permenant deputy (previously unsuccessful)

findings.headline: The council has formally accepted that using reserves to fund operations in future years before Local Government Reorganisation is a reasonable approach
findings.detail: The committee is confirming that reserves will be used to cover shortfalls in future years, and has asked officers to plan for savings outlined in a revised Medium Term Financial Strategy. This indicates structural budget deficits are expected in the lead-up to LGR.
findings.matters: Planned reliance on reserves to fund operations signals structural budget imbalance and erodes the council's financial cushion for unexpected events
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £6.5m, general reserves £8.4m, with core reserve of £2.3m retained as last-resort funding source
findings.quote: use of reserves in future years before Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is a reasonable approach in the current circumstances

findings.headline: The council is using interim staff in Finance and Planning because permanent recruitment is proving highly challenging
findings.detail: Overspending in operational areas is being driven by the need to use interim staff to cover vacant posts in Finance and Planning where recruitment is difficult. This increased temporary staffing cost is offsetting otherwise better financial performance elsewhere in the budget.
findings.matters: Weak permanent staffing in finance reduces financial control and oversight; gaps in planning affect planning fee income collection
findings.figures: Total service net expenditure forecast £43,000 underspend on £12.724m budget, indicating overspends in some areas are being offset elsewhere
findings.quote: Overspending in operational areas is driven by the need to use interim staff to cover vacant posts in key delivery areas where recruitment is proving highly challenging (Planning and Finance).

findings.headline: Governance system change anticipated from Committee to Cabinet model
findings.detail: The council is tracking government indication that Committee systems will cease in preference for Cabinet system of governance. The Planning and Infrastructure Bill also proposes to end area planning committees and introduce planning committee member certification. These changes are being addressed through the Decision Making Accountability methodology review.
findings.matters: Changes to governance structures affect decision-making accountability and oversight quality, relevant to lender assessment of council governance strength and controls.
findings.figures: Completion target: 31/03/2026
findings.quote: A government letter indicating that Committee systems will cease to exist in preference for a Cabinet system of governance, and we are tracking these developments and ensuring governance and decision making is addressed accordingly

findings.headline: Local Government Review business cases to be submitted 26 September 2025
findings.detail: Maldon is developing business cases for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) with submission scheduled for 26 September 2025. The council will then await government decision on potential restructuring. This is tracked as an ongoing action with completion target of 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: LGR could result in significant changes to the council's structure and governance, potentially affecting its future viability, financial position, and borrowing arrangements.
findings.figures: Submission date: 26/09/25; Completion target: 31/03/2026
findings.quote: Business cases are currently being developed for LGR and will be submitted on 26/09/25 we will then await Government decision

news_drafts.headline: Investment income beat budget by 58%, though future returns will face headwind from delayed rate cuts.
news_drafts.lead: Current treasury management is solid and helped offset capital losses, but the interest rate outlook suggests declining future investment returns. For a council planning to externalize £8.552m in borrowing, this compounds the borrowing cost pressure.

news_drafts.headline: Council is under-borrowed by £8.552m and plans to externalize this through PWLB when necessary.
news_drafts.lead: This signals planned PWLB borrowing demand. Treasury advisers now forecast interest rates will hold elevated until Q3 2027, meaning when the council externalizes this borrowing it will face higher-than-previously-expected costs. Lenders need clarity on…

news_drafts.headline: Strategic property funds have fallen in value to £4.532m from £5m invested, representing a £468k capital loss.
news_drafts.lead: Capital losses on strategic investments reduce available reserves and financial resilience. Lenders assessing creditworthiness need to understand how the council's investment strategy has performed and what reserves are genuinely available for stress.
